description: Multidisciplinary team of engineering students from Universidad de La Frontera (UFRO), Chile, at NASA Space Apps 2026 Temuco. Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. We're creating an interactive game where young students manage a lunar or Martian base, balancing oxygen, energy, water, food and crew safety. From biology to technology, we make space exploration fun and accessible.
summary:
Kids know how space missions end, but they almost never decide anything that happens in one. Content for their age stops at posters or gets too technical, and educational content struggles to hold attention.

Michinautas is a web game for ages 7 to 12 built on one rule: the kid makes the mission's decisions and sees what they cost before choosing. A cat astronaut has 7 lunar days to finish a research mission on a Moon base, with five bars that never stretch far enough. Shielding against a flare drains the energy needed for the night, going outside adds radiation, and pedaling trades food for energy. Costs carry over: a crack leaks air every day until it is fixed. Minigames raise what you gain and never lower what you pay.

The Sun is real: each mission replays a week recorded by NASA and NOAA (2019 and 2024), with every flare at its real hour and its class setting the dose. The game compares what you received with what you would have received outside, and says it is a historical archive, not live data. It includes 38 sourced fact sheets.

Losing teaches: the end report explains what happened from the player's choices. It runs in the browser with no account, in Spanish and English, and collects no data.
details:
Michinautas is a browser game for kids aged 7 to 12 that puts them in charge of a Moon base. A cat astronaut has 7 lunar days to finish a research mission with five bars (energy, oxygen, food, health and radiation) that never stretch far enough. Every action shows its cost before the player chooses it. Shielding against a solar flare drains the energy needed for the lunar night, going outside adds radiation, and pedaling trades food for energy. Costs carry over: a crack leaks air every day until it is sealed. Minigames make each task fun, but they only raise what you gain and never lower what you pay.

The Sun is real. Each mission replays a real week (December 2019, May 2024 and October 2024) from NASA DONKI records cross-checked with NASA and NOAA reports. Every flare arrives at its real hour and its class sets the dose. We also use Chang'e 4 lunar radiation, NASA Moon Fact Sheet data and the 2.56 s Earth-Moon signal delay. The game says it is a historical archive, not live data, and 38 fact sheets cite every source.

Benefits and impact: kids don't just read about trade-offs, they make them and see the result. Losing explains what happened instead of punishing. It needs only a link, so any classroom can use it. Each mission won tells a real story of Chile-US space cooperation.

Tools: TypeScript, Phaser 4, Vite, HTML and CSS, Vitest, procedural Web Audio, Python scripts for the art, static hosting on nginx. No special hardware.

Creativity: a paper-cutout cat walks a 2.5D Moon base where every machine is a minigame, and the real Sun is the game's weather.

Factors considered: plain language for ages 7 to 12, no free choices, honest labeling of stored data, accessibility (contrast, touch, reduced motion, light mode) and no personal data collected from children.
